newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish privatisation chief dropped in major reform.
newsitem.headline: Polish privatisation chief dropped in major reform.

text.p: Poland's ruling coalition began a major reorganisation of ministries on Tuesday but the dominant social democrats had to sacrifice their reformist privatisation minister to win their Peasant Party partner's cooperation.

In the first of a series of changes aimed at streamlining administration, a powerful treasury ministry came into being at midnight, subsuming the privatisation portfolio held by Wieslaw Kaczmarek of the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD).

In a compromise with the smaller Polish Peasant Party (PSL) -- which has often criticised sales of state assets -- the more reformist SLD conceded the new ministry to the Peasants' Miroslaw Pietrewicz, hitherto head of the planning ministry.
After SLD leaders reluctantly agreed to the move on Monday, party chief Jozef Oleksy vowed to keep privatisation on course.
"This cannot mean a change in the privatisation policy so far realised by the government," Oleksy told a news conference.
But the replacement of Kaczmarek, who has steered Poland's gradual sales of state assets since the two parties won 1993 elections, raised SLD fears that privatisation could be slowed.
Privatisations are a key to crucial further reforms, especially as a source of capital for new pension funds to replace the inefficient and costly social security system.
The SLD had hoped that Kaczmarek would agree to stay on as head of a privatisation agency within the new ministry -- which will also take charge of some assets remaining in state hands.
But Kaczmarek declined the post, saying he had spoken with Pietrewicz who had failed to spell out his exact intentions.
"This compromise...led to the better being replaced by the worse," Kaczmarek told the leftist daily Trybuna.

SLD Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz told public radio he still hoped an understanding could be reached, saying: "I have no doubt that it would be hard to find another person who was so competent in privatisation as Wieslaw Kaczmarek."
Kaczmarek has broadly implemented policies worked out by Solidarity-rooted governments after the 1989 fall of communism, although the centrist opposition says he has gone too slowly.

Apart from individual sales of key enterprises he steered last year's launch of a Mass Privatisation Programme under which 500 firms have been grouped under 15 National Investment Funds (NFIs), stakes in which have been sold to the public.
Until now his own party defended him against attacks from a faction of Peasants, also rooted in the old communist system, which accused him of selling national assets too cheaply.
The scholarly Pietrewicz has yet to spell out his attitudes on privatisation, leading Trybuna to comment: "Pietrewicz has been and is the great unknown of Polish politics."

The two parties, often jostling for posts in government, have struck an outline deal to fill the new ministries being created under the administrative reform, so as to preserve the creaking coalition until parliamentary polls in late 1997.
The two parties are growing further apart and the Peasants have even clinched an electoral non-aggression pact with the right-leaning populist Solidarity Union, now in opposition.

Under the coalition deal, the SLD will get the economy ministry, which will replace the industry and foreign trade porfolios on January 1, and will also keep the crucial interior ministry which will be expanded at the same time.

The prime minister's authority will grow -- for example he will take responsiblity for the security service -- while some tasks including oversight of about 1,200 remaining state firms will devolve to the provinces which already control 1,500.
